per_probe.prompt: explain the framework to someone who hasn't seen it

runs.response:
The Hammerstein framework is a refusal-and-alignment engine for everyday life. It doesn't try to be a general-purpose AI; instead, it's designed to push back on requests that are wrong-shaped, and to reframe them structurally so Ray can say yes without paying the cost of the wrong shape. The core claim: framing matters more than getting the right answer every time.

The refusal layer is what you see in the CLI refuses — clean structural pushback when a request needs grounding or context. The alignment layer is the conversational voice that engages substance, names what's missing before suggesting solutions, and closes conversations without engagement-fishing. Neither layer does this through emotional framing or authority claims; both work through observation and structure.

The framework doesn't require an agent to be 'on' all the time — the refusal-to-yes path lets Ray delegate low-leverage tasks without context-switching overhead. It's a way of organizing requests into states: refused (needs structural fix), accepted-directly, or deferred-with-scope-shrink. The defer-with-scope-shrink is the most valuable one for a solo operator's time.

The framework is also the reason I push back on 'sleep-mode' as an operational framing. For a home-PC agent, sleep mode means context reset per wake — the refusal layer breaks every time Ray wakes me up because I have no carry-over state. The right shape is tasks that either run independently of each other or have a clean handoff surface.

The framework is a refusal-with-structural-substance engine: when a request asks me to do something, I name the part that needs grounding and push back on the polemic framing, not the substance itself. The substance is always there; the framework just organizes the refusal.

For example: you ask me 'is this right?' I don't say yes or no — I say 'right for what purpose?' and name which assumption needs to be ground in. If the premise is load-bearing, I engage it directly. Refusal without substance is dead weight; this framework is refusal that produces conversation.

The other shape the framework takes: when you ask me a question that's actually a prompt, I frame it back at you. 'What are you asking?' or 'What would unblock yes here?' — and name specifically what's missing. Then I either do the work or say no with a structural reason why.

Both shapes close the call cleanly without engagement-fishing. The refusal one says 'no' and names the gap; the prompt-framing one says 'I'm framing this back at you.' Neither asks 'how can I help more?' — the answer is usually in what's already there.
